Araghchi talks down Qatari visit
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has talked down the significance of a Qatari delegation's visit to Tehran on Friday.
“Such a trip is not unusual at all. Intermediaries are constantly in contact with Iran and the US, holding meetings with both sides and conveying proposals between them,” Araghchi told reporters in Tehran on Sunday.
Qatar, which has sought to mediate between the US and Iran throughout the conflict, has not commented on the talks.

Demonstrators demanded the closure of the Groupe Chimique Tunisien (GCT), the state-owned phosphate complex that has polluted the city’s air and sea for decades.

Pro-Israel Hakeem Jeffries says he will push legislation targeting settler violence
Pro-Israel US Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the first Black speaker of the House of Representatives next year, has pledged to advance legislation targeting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank within the first 100 days of the new Congress.
In an interview with The New York Times, Jeffries said the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act should be among the early legislative priorities, adding that he expected strong support for it within the House Democratic Caucus.
Jeffries also described the devastation inflicted on Palestinian civilians in Gaza as “unacceptable, unsustainable and un-American”, calling for increased humanitarian assistance, medical aid, housing support and access to clean water and air.
Asked whether he supported the proposed Block the Bombs and Stop the Settlements bills, which call for restricting arms sale to Israel and broader sanctions on settlement expansion, Jeffries said he had not taken a position.
On calls to halt US weapons exports used in regional conflicts, he said the current approach was “not sustainable” and needed to change.
More than a million people have signed a petition urging Democrats to reject Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the US House of Representative. An Economist/YouGov poll published last month found that Jeffries had just a 26 percent approval rating among registered voters.
Critics say that one reason Jeffries' popularity has taken a hit is that he is an avid supporter of Israel.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) ranks among his top campaign-financing contributors.
Jeffries said he expects strong support for the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act. (AFP)

after.summary:
Israeli occupation, Iranian interference threat to Lebanese sovereignty, Aoun says
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has accused Iran of meddling in Lebanon's affairs through Hezbollah's weapons and also demanded Israel withdraw from the country's south.
In a speech on the eve of Lebanon's 83rd independence anniversary, Aoun vowed to press ahead with plans to bring all weapons under state control.
Lebanon's sovereignty still faces two threats, he said: "The Israeli occupation of parts of our territory" and foreign interference from "influential elements within the Iranian regime" through weapons and decisions outside the authority of the Lebanese state.
On Israel, Aoun stressed Lebanon's message was clear and direct: "Withdraw from every inch of Lebanese territory. Stop your attacks."
There would be "no occupation ever again", he said. "And no weapons outside the state that... serve the interests of, foreign powers," he added, without naming a specific group.
Such weapons may once have served a purpose, he said, but later imposed a high cost on Lebanon when they came to serve causes beyond its borders.
"You must hand over your weapons," Aoun said.
The Lebanese government has committed to disarming Hezbollah, whose arsenal has long outstripped that of the national army and which has justified its weapons as necessary to resist Israel.
In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement that included the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from territories it occupies in the south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.
But implementation has stalled and Hezbollah has refused to surrender its weapons.
Israel's army still carries out strikes, shelling and detonations in the south, where its forces are operating in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres.
Report by AFP

The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has urged Germany to arrest an Israeli soldier, Almog Keisi, who has been sighted in Luneburg this week, accusing him of war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide in Gaza.

German authorities can exercise jurisdiction over these offences regardless of the suspect’s nationality or where the alleged crimes were committed, the statement read.
HRF said that Keisi participated in the burning of residential buildings in Gaza City’s Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood between 9 and 10 October 2025, following the announcement of a ceasefire agreement and ahead of Israeli forces’ withdrawal from northern Gaza.
According to the complaint, Keisi posted photographs on 10 October showing himself placing explosives around civilian objects and later posing in front of buildings engulfed in flames. Other soldiers from the Givati Brigade also shared photographs of the burning structures, describing the destruction as a celebratory farewell.
HRF said it had geolocated the buildings near Al-Mawhobeen Secondary Female School and cited NASA fire-detection data and satellite imagery as corroborating evidence of the fires and damage.
Dyab Abou Jahjah, HRF’s general director, said: “Germany has received evidence against suspected war criminals before and chose to look away. Meanwhile, it arrests and prosecutes people for waving keffiyehs or chanting slogans against the genocide."
"So the question stands: how long will Germany spend its resources prosecuting those who fight the genocide instead of those who commit it?"

Spain's High Court has released pro-Palestinian activist and US media heir Fergie Chambers on conditional bail, while it considers an extradition request by the US, according to a court ruling released on Friday.
The court said it had decided to release Chambers after US authorities acknowledged what they described as substantial and unintentional errors in the Spanish translation of an FBI agent's sworn statement submitted in support of the extradition request.
On his release, Chambers told Reuters he believed the accusations against him were baseless and politically motivated, adding that he had been alone in a cell for what "felt like a long time".
"I'm glad that this is a step in the right direction," he said.
Chambers added: "At the end of the day, I understand that most of the sacrifice I've had to make is very, very small in relation to the struggle that we are all a part of for the Palestinian people, for their liberation, for their sovereignty, for their respect, for the right to live."
"But in the context of just being alone in a cell all the time, it feels like a long time. I just missed my family. I really missed my family and my friends,” Chambers said.
Chambers, whose family owns Cox Enterprises, was arrested at the request of US authorities on 10 July while on holiday in Ibiza. He has been held in custody ever since on accusations including riot, conspiracy to commit riot and international money laundering. Chambers, whose full name is James Cox Chambers Jr, denies wrongdoing.
Separately, Chambers' lawyers said they were challenging a raid by Irish police on his family home in Dublin, which they said was conducted at the request of US authorities and involved the seizure of electronic devices and other property. His legal team said it would seek judicial review unless authorities clarify the legal basis for the operation.

Cairo-based rights group, Maat for Peace, Development and Human Rights, has called for an explicit ban on the use of white phosphours, which has repeatedly been used by Israel in Gaza and southern Lebanon, Al Jazeera reported.
White phosphorus can cause severe burns, ignite repeatedly and produce intense heat and toxic smoke.
Human rights groups and The New York Times said in June they have documented Israel's use of the chemical white phosphorus over civilian areas in Lebanon.
White phosphorus is not banned under international law, but it is illegal to use the chemical in and near populated areas since it can cause widespread harm. Israel has been accused by the international human rights community for decades of using the substance in a way that puts civilians in danger.
In a working paper submitted at the review session for the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, the group said the current treaty has glaring gaps that allow for the use of white phosphorus.
Following an impasse after talks started on Monday, the conference ran over time and ended early on Saturday, with states agreeing to continue talks aimed at developing measures on lethal autonomous weapons by 2028.

Calls on the Israeli authorities to protect Palestinian olive farmers and ensure they can reach their groves safely have not been acted upon, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said, citing the Humanitarian Country Team.
Instead, in the first nine months of 2026, Israeli authorities uprooted or otherwise damaged more than 10,000 Palestinian-owned trees and saplings across the West Bank, mostly olives, the statement adds.
The Humanitarian Country Team for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which brings together UN bodies and humanitarian NGOs, said more than 400 Israeli settler attacks on the Palestinian olive harvest since September have resulted in casualties or damage to property, including to more than 4,000 trees and saplings.
The number of attacks this year exceeds that recorded in any previous olive harvest season. This year’s harvesting window is closing, the team said, but there is still some time to act.
"Humanitarian NGOs and UN agencies urge the Israeli authorities in the strongest possible terms: end all attacks on Palestinians and their livelihoods, as required by international law. The first-ever US-Russia-China summit produced a thin declaration, and no carve-up of the world. But the format itself - three powers, one table, no Europeans - might matter more than anything they signed.
In February 1945, US President Franklin Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Yalta to settle the shape of the postwar world.
Eight decades later, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat down on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen for the first trilateral meeting ever held among the leaders of the US, China and Russia.
The comparison was irresistible. Yet after roughly 90 minutes of talks, what emerged was far more modest: a four-point joint “Declaration toward Peace”. The statement’s text suggests that what was supposed to be a historic event was mostly just a photo op.
This brings to mind another photograph, one that adorned the front page of The New York Times a quarter of a century ago, during a United Nations summit in New York in September 2000 that was meant to mark the beginning of a new era focused on “Millennium Development Goals”.
Instead of picturing the General Assembly Hall, the newspaper used an image of the leaders of the UN Security Council’s five permanent members around a table outside the summit - conveying to readers exactly who was really running the show.
Twenty-six years later, the number of leaders dropped from five to three; the two Europeans (the UK and France) were missing in action, and along with them, sadly, the entire EU.

Climate justice campaigners have hit out at the draft outcome of the global climate talks, describing it as the “worst” in the conference’s history.
The draft agreement, which outlines the key commitments of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, was stripped of all references to a phase-out of fossil fuels, but backed “accelerating carbon capture, utilisation and storage”, which civil society actors have derided as a “false solution” to climate breakdown.
“It's much weaker language across all fronts, and overall, when we look at it, it’s aggressive, it is backtracking, and it's not going to help developing countries," Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told Middle East Eye.
"Rather, it is going to help the private sector, fossil fuel industry, and that is not what we came here for,” Singh said.
The “cover decision” is an overarching text which summarises the different negotiation outcomes, containing pledges intended to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement.
An initial draft which appeared on Monday was heavily edited, with many of the main commitments, including a transition away from fossil fuels and a $120bn target for finance to help developing countries adapt to the climate crisis, stripped out.
Crucially, the latest text substitutes a commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels” for a pledge to “irreversible global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate resilience”.
The new draft also centres controversial carbon capture technologies, pledging to increase them 20- to 40-fold by 2035.

Maintaining one’s dignity while surviving a sadistically dehumanising campaign targeting civilians was the central preoccupation of the handful of films about Gaza released between 2024 and early 2026.

On a Friday night in the UK city of Leeds, a nurse taps “send”. Thousands of miles away, a phone buzzes in a courtyard in Omdurman, Sudan, and a ledger of trust begins to turn.
She does not think of this as economics. She thinks of it as family obligation - not as finance, and certainly not as policy. Yet the journey of that single payment, from a British bank account to a pot of lentils shared among displaced neighbours, is a map of how Sudan survives.
It is a journey across a collapsing currency. Before the war, a dollar bought roughly 600 Sudanese pounds. Last month it passed 10,000, and the currency is still sliding.
Shopkeepers have shuttered their stores rather than sell at a loss when the rate lurches overnight. Average incomes have fallen to levels last seen in 1992, while government revenues dropped from roughly 10 percent of GDP in 2022 to below five in 2024.
Banks are closed across conflict zones, supply chains have snapped, and the state has little left to offer. In this vacuum, ordinary Sudanese have built something else.
The mechanics are unforgiving. Sudan imports most of its wheat, so every fall in the pound affects the price of bread; bakeries in Khartoum have closed as wheat and fuel costs climb. The country’s finance minister attributes the slide to demand for dollars as imports outstrip exports.

Confidence in Hormuz has been 'crushed' by war on Iran, IEA says
The US-Israeli war on Iran has “crushed” confidence in the Strait of Hormuz as a reliable waterway for the export of energy, Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA), has warned.
“I don’t see any credible pathway back to the situation that existed in February 2026,” Birol wrote for The Economist magazine in an essay published on Wednesday.
“Shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz have been blocked once, with a hugely disruptive effect on oil and gas markets. It can happen again. Confidence in the Strait as a safe and reliable corridor for energy and other goods has been crushed,” he added.
Birol said that the world "can conceivably manage without the strait," but it would be "difficult".
In its World Energy Outlook report published on Thursday, the IEA said developing alternative pipelines around the waterway would require around $40bn. This would add around $2 to the cost of a barrel of oil exported from the Middle East. An additional $200bn would need to be spent on alternative sources of energy outside the Middle East.
The IEA said that in the case of oil alone, new pipeline projects are under construction or consideration in the Middle East that could pump around seven million barrels per day of oil, allowing producers to reach international markets without going through the strait.

Senate vote to curb Trump war on Iran fails again
For the 15th time this year, the US Senate has tried to curb President Donald Trump's warmaking authority in Iran. It succeeded twice, once in May and once in June, but failed on Thursday by a vote of 51-48.
Fifty Republicans and Democratic Senator John Fetterman voted against the resolution, while only 43 Democrats were present to vote in favour. They were joined by two Independents, and three Republicans in Rand Paul, Lisa Murkowski, and Susan Collins.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who previously voted alongside Democrats, suggested the repeat votes were becoming fruitless, telling reporters on Thursday that there should be "more weight on solving the fundamental problem" instead.
Tillis decided not to run in this month's midterm elections after a spate of Trump-led attacks on him last year. He will now be replaced by Democrat Roy Cooper, the senator-elect, in North Carolina.
The election results were a decisive rebuke of the Trump administration's domestic and foreign policy, as Vice President JD Vance himself acknowledged the very next day.
Trump has previously just ignored the two successful resolutions stipulating that only Congress has the authority to declare - and thereby fund - the US at war.
The move effectively rendered the Senate's efforts moot.

Houthis hit Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund skyscraper
The skyscraper housing Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) in Riyadh was damaged on Thursday by a Houthi strike, the kingdom has confirmed.
The strike destroyed windows across seven to eight floors of the tower, Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, and bent part of its metal facade, according to a Reuters journalist. Video footage shared from the Saudi capital showed crews already working to replace the glass.
The attack is the second time this month that the Houthis have struck at the heart of Saudi Arabia’s image as a safe investment destination. PIF says it has around $1 trillion in assets. Earlier this month, the Houthis struck Aramco Tower in Riyadh.
“One of the towers of the Financial Center in Riyadh was targeted in a terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia, causing material damage but no injuries -praise be to God,” the Saudi authorities said in a statement released on Thursday.
The press release included an image showing notable but relatively minor damage to the PIF headquarters. Video footage appeared to show a missile slamming into the 80-storey tower, but Middle East Eye could not independently verify the footage.

Somalia has ordered the UAE ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours, and recalled his Somali counterpart from Abu Dhabi, citing an "open invasion" against "the sovereignty, security, land and unity of the Somalis".
Information Minister Abdifatah Kasim Mohamud announced the decision at a news conference in the Somali capital Mogadishu, warning that "measures will be taken against anyone who cooperates with the UAE in the invasion against Somalia".
“All Somalis are urged to defend their country and unite against the open invasion of the UAE against the sovereignty, security, land and unity of Somalis,” he said, not elaborating on what provoked the expulsion.
There was no immediate response from the Emirati foreign ministry, but diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, Anwar Gargash, condemned the comments in a post on X as an “attack”, which he said “reflects the shifting nature of his positions and policies, and raises questions about his prioritisation of personal calculations over his country’s national interests”.
Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on Tuesday accused the UAE of interference" in his country's internal affairs, and alleged Abu Dhabi was backing armed groups and fuelling divisions between the federal government and regional administrations.

A UK school trust has apologised and agreed to pay compensation to four children who were threatened with referrals to the government’s counterterrorism Prevent programme after wearing Palestinian colours and badges at a school charity event.
The children attended Barclay Primary School in Leyton, east London, in November 2023, when they wore Palestinian colours in memory of children killed in Gaza during the school’s Children in Need event.
The primary school is part of the Lion Academy Trust, which runs 11 primary academies in east London.
Following the event, the children's parents received letters warning that they could be referred to Prevent or to the police’s hate crime unit for wearing the Palestine flag or its colours, which it deemed “overt demonstrations of political beliefs” that could be “deemed offensive".
Middle East Eye understands that the letter was sent to the families of a number of children, including an eight-year-old who lost 14 members of his family in Gaza.
Prevent Watch, which has supported the families throughout its three-year legal battle, confirmed to MEE that a court approved the settlement on Thursday after the families, represented by law firm Leigh Day, brought claims under the Equality Act 2010 and the Human Rights Act 1998.
The case has renewed concerns about the use of the UK’s counterterrorism framework in educational settings and the treatment of Palestinian solidarity in schools.
The Lion Academy Trust did not respond to MEE's request for comment at the time of publication.

Two Palestinians killed, several injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza
Two Palestinians were killed and several others injured on Thursday in Israeli attacks targeting multiple areas across the Gaza Strip.
Citing eyewitnesses, Wafa news reported that an Israeli drone opened fire on a group of Palestinians on Salah al-Din Street, southeast of Gaza City, killing one person instantly.
Another Palestinian was killed when Israeli artillery shelled the Zeitoun neighbourhood east of Gaza City with several rounds.
Meanwhile, two Palestinians, including a child, were injured by Israeli gunfire at the Siham School west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, and another was injured in an Israeli drone strike on Bahloul station, a shelter for displaced people east of Gaza City.
